title: Early favorable prostate-specific antigen response prediction in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer

paper_content.abstract: There is an unmet need for a tool that could predict early favorable prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) patients receiving androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Here, we train and validate a multivariable logistic regression model to predict early favorable PSA response (≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months) in these patients. Patients randomly allocated to the ARPI arms of the LATITUDE (abiraterone), TITAN (apalutamide), and ARASENS (darolutamide) trials, are split 60:40 into training (n = 1030) and internal validation (n = 688) cohorts. The locked model is validated in an independent external validation cohort - the enzalutamide arm of the ENZAMET trial (n = 540). The area under curve and Brier score for the locked model in the external validation cohort are 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.78–0.85) and 0.16, respectively. Stratification by predicted probability tertiles show PSA response rates of 92% (95% CI = 88–96), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 39% (95% CI = 32–47), respectively. Pending prospective validation, our model predicts early favorable PSA response supporting its potential role in guiding treatment decisions.
paper_content.introduction:
Early PSA response is a well-established prognostic marker in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) patients treated with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) alone or a combination of ADT plus androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPI) with or without docetaxel1–7. Achieving a PSA response of ≤0.2 ng/mL within 6 months of treatment initiation predicts improved overall survival (OS) and mediates the treatment effect on subsequent mortality risk8. Conversely, failure to reach this response threshold portends inferior OS. Therefore, this clinical state may warrant an earlier treatment intensification, or a clinical trial enrollment. However, waiting until 6 months to assess PSA nadir may inadvertently delay timely intervention, allowing disease progression and evolution to a more treatment-resistant state, potentially diminishing the benefit of subsequent therapeutic intensification. Predicting PSA responses using pre-treatment variables, especially in ARPI-treated patients, could enable earlier, personalized treatment decisions before the optimal intervention window closes.

Conventional risk stratification methods in mHSPC, such as volume of metastatic disease based on conventional imaging9,10, have limited accuracy in predicting early PSA response. For example, one study demonstrated that over half of patients with favorable PSA responses had high-volume metastatic disease, while nearly 1/3 of those with suboptimal PSA response had low-volume disease8. These findings underscore the limitations of relying on a single variable for risk stratification and treatment optimization in mHSPC.

Therefore, there is an unmet need of an easily deployable clinical tool, which could predict favorable early PSA response. While such tool will not be a replacement for formal PSA monitoring, it will provide baseline prognostic insights that can enhance early risk stratification, guide treatment planning, and support enrollment in biomarker-driven studies.

In this work, we developed and validated the Nadir ARPI-Derived Integrative Response (NADIR) model using individual patient data from four phase III trials (ARASENS, ENZAMET, LATITUDE, and TITAN)11–14. This tool leverages pretreatment clinical and laboratory parameters to estimate the likelihood of achieving a PSA ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of initiating ARPI-based therapy.
paper_content.results:
Baseline characteristics
Overall, 1718 male patients were treated with ARPI agents in the ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials, of whom the training cohort consisted of 1030 patients, while the internal validation cohort consisted of 688 patients. The external validation cohort consisted of 540 male patients from the ENZAMET trial (Fig. 1). Baseline characteristics have been summarized in Supplementary Table S1 (supplementary information). Overall, 54% (n = 551) in the training cohort, 56% (n = 383) in the internal validation cohort, and 69% (n = 371) in the external validation cohort experienced an early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months.

Modeltrainingandvalidation
After the NADIR model (https://bit.ly/42Ec1lP) was built utilizing the training cohort, it was locked and applied to the two validation cohorts. The model coefficients with 95% confidence intervals (CI) are summarized in Table 1. In the internal validation cohort, the AUC for the NADIR model was 0.76 (95% CI = 0.72–0.79) with a Brier score of 0.20. In the external validation cohort, the AUC was 0.82 (95% CI = 0.78–0.85) with a Brier score of 0.16. The receiver operating curves are shown in Fig. 2. The calibration plots showed alignment between the predicted probabilities and the actual outcomes in the training, internal and external validation cohorts (Supplementary Figs. S1, S2, S3, respectively, in the supplementary information). In the external validation cohort, the sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV of the model were 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.86), 0.62 (95% CI = 0.54–0.69), 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.86), and 0.62 (95% CI = 0.54–0.69), respectively (Supplementary Table S2, supplementary information). On LOOCV, the model demonstrated consistent performance (AUC values ranging between 0.78 and 0.82; Brier scores ranging from 0.16 to 0.19) across trials (Supplementary Table S3, supplementary information). There was substantial heterogeneity in the distribution of predicted probability of achieving early PSA response based on metastatic volume by CHAARTED definition across the internal validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S4, supplementary information) and external validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S5, supplementary information), respectively. Removing baseline PSA from the multivariable model led to a substantial drop in predictive accuracy in external validation, confirming PSA as an important predictor but not a sufficient one (Table 2). Importantly, the full NADIR model outperformed PSA-only model across exploratory subgroups within the external validation cohort stratified by baseline PSA levels with greater benefits among patients with baseline PSA value higher than 5 ng/mL (Supplementary Table S4, supplementary information).

RiskstratificationbyNADIRmodel
When stratified by decreasing order of tertiles of predicted probability of early PSA response, the proportions achieving a favorable early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL in the upper (n = 229), middle (n = 229), and lower tertile (n = 230) were 83% (95% CI = 78–88), 52% (95% CI = 46–59), and 32% (95% CI = 26–38) in the internal validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S6, supplementary information). Similarly, the proportions achieving a favorable early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL in the upper (n = 180), middle (n = 180), and lower tertile (n = 180) were 92% (95% CI = 88–96), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 39% (95% CI = 32–47) in the external validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S7, supplementary information). Quartile-based stratification demonstrated similar differences in the proportion of patients with early favorable PSA responses in the internal and external validation cohort, respectively (Supplementary Figs. S8 and S9, supplementary information). On decision curve analysis in the external validation cohort, the NADIR model was most useful for identifying patients at a range of risk that is clinically meaningful (threshold probabilities between 25% and 60%) for early PSA drop in patients treated with ARPI with a higher net benefit in this range compared to both baseline assumptions (no patient has early PSA response, and all patients have early PSA response) (Supplementary Fig. S10, supplementary information).

We subsequently determined the OS estimates across the tertiles of predicted probability from the NADIR model using Kaplan–Meier methods. The 4-years OS probabilities in patients stratified by tertiles of predicted probability were 71% (95% CI = 65–79); 61% (95% CI = 55–69); and 47% (95% CI = 39–56), respectively in the internal validation cohort (n = 672) (Fig. 3) and 80% (95% CI = 75–86), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 56% (95% CI = 49–64), respectively in the external validation cohort (n = 540) (Fig. 4). On Cox proportional hazard regression modeling, compared to upper tertile, patients in the middle and lower tertile had inferior OS in the internal validation cohort (HR for middle tertile = 1.57 [95% CI = 1.11–2.21]; HR for lower tertile = 2.28 [95% CI = 1.65–3.16]) and in the external validation cohort (HR for middle tertile = 1.35 [95% CI = 0.92–1.69]; HR for lower tertile = 2.72 [95% CI = 1.91–3.88], respectively.

Exploratoryanalysisofinteractionwithdocetaxeleffect
In the combined validation cohort, we did not find any considerable evidence of difference in proportion of patients with early PSA response with and without use of docetaxel across the three risk score groups (Supplementary Table S5, supplementary information). We found a differential effect from docetaxel on OS across the predicted scores from the NADIR model (HR for the interaction term 0.41; 95% CI = 0.19–0.88; two-sided p-interaction = 0.0215) (Supplementary Fig. S11, supplementary information). Kaplan–Meier method-based OS estimates with and without docetaxel use in these groups are shown in Supplementary Figs. S12 and S13, respectively (supplementary information). For patients in the lower tertile of predicted probability of early favorable PSA response (n = 401), 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 55% (95% CI = 48–63) and 53% (95% CI = 46–61), respectively while for patients in the upper to middle tertiles (n = 811), the 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 66% (95% CI = 60–72) and 72% (95% CI = 68–77), respectively (Supplementary Fig. S12, supplementary information). For patients in the upper-tertile of predicted probability of early favorable PSA response (n = 408), 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 72% (95% CI = 65–80) and 78% (95% CI = 72–83), respectively while for patients in the lower to middle tertiles (n = 804), 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 58% (95% CI = 52–63) and 60% (95% CI = 56–65), respectively (Supplementary Fig. S13, supplementary information). Similar evidence of differential treatment effect from on OS across the predicted scores from the NADIR model (HR for the interaction term 0.28; 95% CI = 0.09–0.92; two-sided p-interaction = 0.03377) was found in the external validation cohort (n = 540) (Supplementary Fig. S14, supplementary information).

Additionalsensitivityanalyses
As an exploratory analysis, we applied the NADIR model on patients treated with ADT with/without docetaxel. In patients treated with ADT with/without docetaxel, the AUC of the NADIR model was 0.77 (95% CI = 0.75–0.79) with a Brier score of 0.24. On decision curve analysis, the NADIR model was useful for identifying patients at a range of risk that is clinically meaningful (threshold probabilities between 15% and 50%) for early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months (Supplementary Fig. S15, supplementary information). On sensitivity analysis, the random forest classifier model had an AUC and Brier scores similar to the logistic regression model in the internal validation cohort (AUC: 0.75 [95% CI = 0.72–0.80]; Brier score: 0.20) and in the external validation cohort (AUC: 0.83 [95% CI = 0.79–0.86]; Brier score: 0.17), respectively. Additional metrics for the random forest classifier model are summarized in Supplementary Table S6 (supplementary information). The decision curve analysis showed similar net benefit as the logistic regression model when compared to both baseline assumptions (Supplementary Fig. S16, supplementary information).
paper_content.methods:
Studycohorts
Our research complies with all relevant ethical regulations by the institutional review board of University Hospitals Seidman Cancer Center (STUDY20251115) and data-sharing agreements with trial sponsors. All patients provided informed consent before they were enrolled in the respective trials. A literature search was performed using Medline and Clinicaltrials.gov to identify phase III randomized controlled trials of patients solely with mHSPC randomized to ADT with or without an ARPI, irrespective of docetaxel use. Each trial group or industry partner was contacted to obtain IPD. Four trials met criteria for which IPD access was granted for analysis: ARASENS (NCT02799602), ENZAMET (NCT02446405), LATITUDE (NCT01715285), and TITAN (NCT02489318). For ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN, data were accessed via a peer-reviewed data access request on the Vivli platform (Project ID: 009912), while data from the ENZAMET (NCT02446405) trial were accessed through the Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group. This post-hoc analysis was conducted in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan approved by all relevant parties.

Patients eligible for this analysis were adult (≥18 years) patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed mHSPC, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status score of 0 or 1, and evidence of metastases on bone scans or cross-sectional imaging. All study participants were male, and sex was determined by clinical diagnosis. Patients were included if they were randomly assigned to and treated with ADT with or without docetaxel plus ARPI and had complete baseline and follow-up data for clinical outcomes, treatment assignments, and baseline (pre-ARPI) demographic and clinical characteristics, and laboratory variables such as age (in years), body mass index (BMI), metastatic disease volume (high versus low per CHAARTED criteria)9,10, visceral metastases (yes/no), baseline PSA (ng/mL), hemoglobin (g/L), docetaxel use (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous), respectively. All analyzes complied with the terms set by the data providers, and no identifiable patient information was used.

Statisticsandreproducibility
The primary endpoint was early favorable PSA response, defined as a decline in serum PSA level to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of random allocation among patients treated with an ARPI. Patients from ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials were pooled and randomly split into training (60%) and internal validation (40%) cohorts using unstratified random allocation. We used a 60:40 split to prioritize a larger training cohort for model development, ensuring stable coefficient estimation while retaining a sufficiently large internal validation cohort for performance testing. The training cohort was used to build the model and once locked, the model’s performance was evaluated in the internal and external validation cohorts.

Model development utilized logistic regression, including baseline PSA fitted with restricted cubic splines with 4 degrees of freedom, log of baseline hemoglobin, baseline body mass index, and age at enrollment respectively, in addition to metastatic disease volume (low versus high by CHAARTED definition)9, visceral metastasis (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous). Variables election was based on clinical relevance, with final model specification determined by the Akaike Information Criterion. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals from 5000 bootstrap iterations. Calibration was evaluated by comparing bootstrapped estimates of early PSA nadir probabilities with 95% confidence intervals across tertiles of predicted probabilities in both internal and external validation cohorts. We selected tertiles to ensure adequate sample sizes and event counts within each subgroup. This avoided over-stratification, which could lead to unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals. Additional performance metrics included Brier score (which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities with lower Brier score indicating better calibration), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and positive and negative likelihood ratio. No pre-specified probability threshold was selected to define clinical actionability; thresholds were explored post hoc to evaluate model performance across a range of values using decision curve analysis. Variable importance was estimated using loss of index of prediction accuracy (IPA). IPA is calculated by rescaling the Brier score.

External validation employed individual patient data from the ARPI arm of the ENZAMET trial to assess the model’s generalizability. A post-hoc power analysis confirmed adequate sample size to detect an AUC of 0.75 with a significance level of 0.05. To determine the validation of our model, we performed a leave-one-trial-out-validation (LOOCV). Each trial was sequentially excluded and used as an external validation cohort while the model was trained on the remaining three trials. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the AUC with 95% confidence intervals. Calibration was evaluated using Brier scores. This approach allows for evaluation of model generalizability and reduces potential overfitting to any single dataset. As an additional sensitivity analysis, a random forest classifier was developed and evaluated using the same framework.

Given the prognostic implications of early PSA response, overall survival (OS) was explored in a 6-month landmark population stratified by tertiles (upper, middle, and lower) of predicted probability from the NADIR model. Overall survival (OS) was reported at 4 years because follow-up beyond 4 years was limited in the training and validation cohorts. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated hazard of deaths across the tertiles, and the potential differential effect of docetaxel based on predicted probabilities from the NADIR model using an interaction term. Proportionality assumption was tested using Grambsch–Therneau test. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was made, and all reported p-values were 2-sided. All statistical analyzes were performed using R version 4.4.1 with its associated packages (tidymodels, tidyverse, pROC, riskRegression, survival, rms)37–40.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Reviewer Manuscript Overview:
This research is significant for its potential practical implications for improving the health and lives of patients with metastatic
hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC). The study is highly motivated and builds upon an extensive body of literature
that establishes a strong link between early, deep PSA response and better long-term clinical outcomes, including overall
survival, in mHSPC patients.
The overall methods and approach are suitable for the prediction model and research purposes (barring additional
questions/comments I provided below). I commend in particular the efforts of the authors to obtain and utilize individual
patient data (IPD) from each of the four pivotal mHSPC ARPI trials, as these efforts were instrumental in ensuring potential
study/model robustness and reliability.
Reviewer Comments and Questions:
Comments by Manuscript Page and Line Number
• Pg 13 15 – Why was baseline PSA fitted with restricted cubic splines with 4 DoF? Please clearly explain and justify the
rationale given this particularly specific fit.
• Pg 13 19 – How about Gleason Score? Considerations for controlling given its link to PSA response and longer term
clinical outcomes?
• Pg 13 19 – A key covariate/potential confounding factor that comes to mind for me is the temporal differences between the
trials. For example, changes in standard of care (in LPC and mPC), advanced/next generation imaging (NGS) to detect
mPC, and other changes in recommended clinical care in this disease area between the time say LATITUDE and
ARASENS were conducted. Suggest to control for time or year of treatment (or initiation) across patient and trial cohorts or
provide rationale for it’s not controlled for.
• Pg 13 20 – Why was AIC used to select model variables? Any considerations for Elastic Net, LASSO, or other ML
approaches for variable selection to better handle potential overfitting or multicollinearity?
• Pg 14 2 – Why were tertiles chosen, as opposed to say quartiles for example? Either is fine, but would be helpful to provide
a justification.
• Pg 16 6 – What’s most interesting to me is that the greatest relative gains in the model were for patients in the middle 5-50
ng/mL group, suggest calling this out. Any ideas why this group has biggest relative gain in accuracy for the model?
• Pg 16 20 – Why were 4-year OS probabilities modeled instead of the typical 5-year OS? Fine if due to data limitations or
follow-up counts, but please justify in the text if so.
• Figure E6.1/E6.2 Interesting that the survival probability for upper-middle tertiles is higher for patients without docetaxel
(72%) than with docetaxel (66%) (E6.1) and in upper tertile (72% and 78%) (E6.2), at least descriptively. Why is this the
case, residual confounding of patient characteristics? Maybe helpful to call out in manuscript, beyond the general limitation
(given the relatively large difference).
Major Comments on Overall Methodology
• My biggest question or concern is the lack of justification around why ENZAMET was specifically used for the external
validation dataset. Some commonly established challenges and drawbacks of using only one trial/database for external
validation (ENZAMET) include the potential for: overfitting risk and reduced generalizability, especially if additional
differences between the internal training/external validation samples (e.g., patient characteristics, years of trial, etc.)
I would suggest the use of leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), which would aggregate model fit by using and rotating
each of the 4 pivotal trial databases as the external validation arm, which can help reduce the potential for dataset-specific
overfitting and bolster model generalizability with more equitable model evaluation across the 4 trial datasets.
• IF it is not feasible for LOOCV or a more generalizable test/training validation to be done, or if there’s a rationale that
supports the given internal/external validation approach (with one external dataset) vs. LOOCV or other approaches, then
please be sure to provide adequate explanation and justification for your current approach of training/testing and why the
authors identified this as the best method and approach. Also, please give a strong rationale and justification for why
ENZAMET specifically was chosen as external validation cohort, of the four pivotal Phase 3 trials, and update the limitations
section as applicable.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Dr. Roy et al. described a novel tool developed to identify early favorable PSA response in mHSPC
patients who would benefit from early treatment personalization. They used mHSPC patients treated on ADT+ARPI arm of
LATITUDE, TITAN, ARANSES trials (training and internal validation cohort), and ENZAMET (as external validation cohort).
They concluded that their model satisfactorily predicts early favorable PSA response (≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months) and needs
prospective validation.
The reviewer has the following comments:
1. Please describe the randomization process of pooled data into training (60%) and internal validation (40%) cohorts. Is
there a reason for 60%:40 % randomization vs 50%: 50% (which may seem logical).
2. The ENZAMET trial had a planned evaluation of participants (including PSA) every 12 weeks, and allowed prior
docetaxel, which is different from other pooled trials, which are industry-sponsored and had more PSA data in the first 6
months. Is there a reason why ENZAMET was selected as an external validation cohort? Please comment.
3. Discussion (Page 19). What are the values of PSA of “patients with lower baseline PSA values” and “patients with higher
baseline PSA values. Please be more specific.
4. The number of figures is extensive. For instance, Figures E1.1, E1.2, and E4 can be moved to the supplementary figures.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Author Response 1st Revision:
On behalf of my co-authors, I would like to thank the reviewers for the time taken to
critically appraise this manuscript and for allowing us the opportunity to respond to their
comments. We have addressed, item by item, the reviewers’ comments, with responses
appearing below. Given the concern on validation, we have performed the leave-one-
trial-out validation in line with the reviewer suggestion. The model continues to show
good discrimination and calibration. Further, we have shortened the abstract to comply
with the word count limits. Revisions have been made to the manuscript with changes
tracked and highlighted, and we have submitted the revised marked manuscript. The
page and line numbers in our responses refer to the marked manuscript.
Reviewer 1
Reviewer Comments:
Comment 1: Why was baseline PSA fitted with restricted cubic splines with 4 DoF?
Please clearly explain and justify the rationale given this particularly specific fit.
Authors’ response: We tested models without splines and with spline degrees of
freedom (DoF) ranging from 3 to 5. The model with 4 DoF achieved the lowest AIC and
thus was chosen for this model. We have mentioned in our manuscript that “Variable
selection was based on clinical relevance, with final model specification determined by
the Akaike Information Criterion” on page no: 5, line no: 115 to 117.
Comment 2: How about Gleason Score? Considerations for controlling given its link to
PSA response and longer term clinical outcomes?
Authors’ response: We agree with the reviewer that Gleason score does hold some
prognostic value in metastatic prostate cancer. However, pre-ARPI Gleason score was
not readily available across the included trials. Further, the reported Gleason scores did
not account for difference between clinical Gleason scores from biopsy versus that
derived from prostatectomy, old versus new grading system, and the differences in
reporting pattern across various countries given these trials were multi-national. For
example, Canada and UK report synoptic Gleason score while USA reports maximum
Gleason score. For these reasons, we elected not to include Gleason score in our
model. We have acknowledged this limitation in the revised manuscript (page no: 15,
line no: 335).
Comment 3: A key covariate/potential confounding factor that comes to mind for me is
the temporal differences between the trials. For example, changes in standard of care
(in LPC and mPC), advanced/next generation imaging (NGS) to detect mPC, and other
changes in recommended clinical care in this disease area between the time say
LATITUDE and ARASENS were conducted. Suggest to control for time or year of
treatment (or initiation) across patient and trial cohorts or provide rationale for it’s not
controlled for.
Authors’ response: We appreciate the reviewer’s point regarding temporal differences
between trials. While an excellent point, fundamentally this will always exist given the
time between trial design and reporting of results in mHSPC trials will be 7+ years (1-2
years to design and activate trial, 2-5 years to enroll, 3-5+ years of follow-up).
Fortunately, all four included trials have established the standard-of-care (SOC)
systemic therapies for mHSPC and collectively define the evidence base guiding current
practice, thereby reducing variability in therapeutic context. Importantly, our leave one
out cross validation (LOOCV) analysis inherently addresses temporal heterogeneity, as
each trial (spanning different eras) served as an independent validation cohort,
demonstrating consistent performance across time frames. The LOOCV analysis is
described on page no: 6, line no: 135 to 140 and reported on page no: 8, line no: 182 to
184. We have also highlighted in the discussion that while these trials underpin the
present SOC, emerging tools such as PET imaging and evolving treatment paradigms
are not fully captured (page no: 15, line no: 328 to 334), and future work will evaluate
model performance in these contexts.
Comment 4: Why was AIC used to select model variables? Any considerations for
Elastic Net, LASSO, or other ML approaches for variable selection to better handle
potential overfitting or multicollinearity?
Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We used AIC for variable
selection because it provides a well-established, information-theoretic framework that
balances model fit and complexity, favoring parsimony and reducing the risk of
overfitting. This approach is widely applied in clinical prediction model development
where interpretability and generalizability are essential. As part of our sensitivity
analyses, we evaluated machine learning methods, including Random Forests, which
are robust to multicollinearity and capable of modeling complex nonlinear relationships.
Random Forest achieved performance similar to our AIC-based logistic regression
model in the external validation cohort (AUC: 0.83 [0.79-0.86] vs 0.82 [0.78-0.85]; Brier
score: 0.17 vs 0.16), confirming that our simpler logistic regression model achieved
comparable accuracy (page no: 11, line no: 243 to 245 and supplementary results R2).
Given its superior interpretability and ease of clinical implementation, we prioritized the
logistic regression model while acknowledging that more complex approaches did not
offer meaningful incremental benefit (page no: 12, line no: 259 to 261).
Comment 5: Why were tertiles chosen, as opposed to say quartiles for example? Either
is fine, but would be helpful to provide a justification.
Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for this observation. We selected tertiles to
ensure adequate sample sizes and event counts within each subgroup. This avoided
over-stratification, which could lead to unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals.
We have mentioned this on page no: 6, line no: 122 to 124. To confirm robustness, we
performed a sensitivity analysis using quartile-based stratification (page no: 9, line no:
198 to 201; supplementary figure 4.1 and 4.2), which showed similar trends, supporting
our choice of tertiles for the primary analysis.
Comment 6: What’s most interesting to me is that the greatest relative gains in the
model were for patients in the middle 5-50 ng/mL group, suggest calling this out. Any
ideas why this group has biggest relative gain in accuracy for the model?
Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation, which led us to
re-examine the IPA values across baseline PSA strata. During this process, we
identified that the previously reported IPA for the multivariable logistic regression model
(NADIR model) in the >50 ng/mL PSA group was not updated from an earlier draft
version of the table during manuscript assembly. This was a reporting oversight that did
not affect the main aspects of analysis or the primary findings.
The correct IPA for the NADIR model in this group is 10.9, compared to 6.0 for the PSA-
only model. With this corrected, the NADIR model demonstrates consistently greater
predictive accuracy than the PSA-only model across all three PSA subgroups (≤5
ng/mL, >5–50 ng/mL, >50 ng/mL), with relatively higher incremental gains in those with
PSA >5 ng/mL. We have verified all other subgroup results and confirm their accuracy.
The manuscript has been updated accordingly, and we appreciate the reviewer’s
comment for helping us strengthen the clarity and accuracy of our report.
Comment 7: Why were 4-year OS probabilities modeled instead of the typical 5-year
OS? Fine if due to data limitations or follow-up counts, but please justify in the text if so.
Authors’ response: We appreciate this comment. As the reviewer highlighted, the follow-
up was limited beyond 4 years in the training and validation cohorts. This is why we
reported the 4-year overall survival estimates. We have now mentioned this clearly in
our statistical consideration section – “Overall survival (OS) was reported at 4 years
because follow-up beyond 4 years was limited in the training and validation cohorts.
(page no: 7, line no: 145 to 147)”. Further, while 5 year OS estimates are preferred in
the context of oncology, studies on metastatic prostate cancer have often reported 3-
year overall survival estimates.
Comment 8: Interesting that the survival probability for upper-middle tertiles is higher
for patients without docetaxel (72%) than with docetaxel (66%) (E6.1) and in upper
tertile (72% and 78%) (E6.2), at least descriptively. Why is this the case, residual
confounding of patient characteristics? Maybe helpful to call out in manuscript, beyond
the general limitation (given the relatively large difference).
Authors’ response: We agree with the astute comment from the reviewer. We have
described the 4-year OS estimates in the text (page no: 10, line no: 224 to 232).
Further, we have discussed this finding in the discussion – “In our study, we did not
observe an OS benefit with addition of docetaxel in those with a relatively higher
predicted probability of early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months. Given the post-
hoc exploratory nature, potential for residual confounding, and the lack of a trial
randomizing to ADT+ARPI +/- docetaxel, this finding is merely hypothesis generating
and is liable to both type I and type II errors. Furthermore, patients referred for
docetaxel on trial might had other poor risk features not captured in the model which
needs further exploration with additional biomarkers (page no: 14, line no: 311 to 317).”
Comment 9: Major Comments on Overall Methodology
My biggest question or concern is the lack of justification around why ENZAMET was
specifically used for the external validation dataset. Some commonly established
challenges and drawbacks of using only one trial/database for external validation
(ENZAMET) include the potential for: overfitting risk and reduced generalizability,
especially if additional differences between the internal training/external validation
samples (e.g., patient characteristics, years of trial, etc.)
I would suggest the use of leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), which would
aggregate model fit by using and rotating each of the 4 pivotal trial databases as the
external validation arm, which can help reduce the potential for dataset-specific
overfitting and bolster model generalizability with more equitable model evaluation
across the 4 trial datasets.
If it is not feasible for LOOCV or a more generalizable test/training validation to be done,
or if there’s a rationale that supports the given internal/external validation approach
(with one external dataset) vs. LOOCV or other approaches, then please be sure to
provide adequate explanation and justification for your current approach of
training/testing and why the authors identified this as the best method and approach.
Also, please give a strong rationale and justification for why ENZAMET specifically was
chosen as external validation cohort, of the four pivotal Phase 3 trials, and update the

## Abstract

There is an unmet need for a tool that could predict early favorable prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) patients receiving androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Here, we train and validate a multivariable logistic regression model to predict early favorable PSA response (≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months) in these patients. Patients randomly allocated to the ARPI arms of the LATITUDE (abiraterone), TITAN (apalutamide), and ARASENS (darolutamide) trials, are split 60:40 into training (n = 1030) and internal validation (n = 688) cohorts. The locked model is validated in an independent external validation cohort - the enzalutamide arm of the ENZAMET trial (n = 540). The area under curve and Brier score for the locked model in the external validation cohort are 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.78–0.85) and 0.16, respectively. Stratification by predicted probability tertiles show PSA response rates of 92% (95% CI = 88–96), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 39% (95% CI = 32–47), respectively. ## Introduction

Early PSA response is a well-established prognostic marker in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) patients treated with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) alone or a combination of ADT plus androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPI) with or without docetaxel1–7. Achieving a PSA response of ≤0.2 ng/mL within 6 months of treatment initiation predicts improved overall survival (OS) and mediates the treatment effect on subsequent mortality risk8. Conversely, failure to reach this response threshold portends inferior OS. Therefore, this clinical state may warrant an earlier treatment intensification, or a clinical trial enrollment. However, waiting until 6 months to assess PSA nadir may inadvertently delay timely intervention, allowing disease progression and evolution to a more treatment-resistant state, potentially diminishing the benefit of subsequent therapeutic intensification. Predicting PSA responses using pre-treatment variables, especially in ARPI-treated patients, could enable earlier, personalized treatment decisions before the optimal intervention window closes.

Conventional risk stratification methods in mHSPC, such as volume of metastatic disease based on conventional imaging9,10, have limited accuracy in predicting early PSA response. For example, one study demonstrated that over half of patients with favorable PSA responses had high-volume metastatic disease, while nearly 1/3 of those with suboptimal PSA response had low-volume disease8. These findings underscore the limitations of relying on a single variable for risk stratification and treatment optimization in mHSPC.

Therefore, there is an unmet need of an easily deployable clinical tool, which could predict favorable early PSA response. While such tool will not be a replacement for formal PSA monitoring, it will provide baseline prognostic insights that can enhance early risk stratification, guide treatment planning, and support enrollment in biomarker-driven studies.

In this work, we developed and validated the Nadir ARPI-Derived Integrative Response (NADIR) model using individual patient data from four phase III trials (ARASENS, ENZAMET, LATITUDE, and TITAN)11–14. This tool leverages pretreatment clinical and laboratory parameters to estimate the likelihood of achieving a PSA ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of initiating ARPI-based therapy.

Overall, 1718 male patients were treated with ARPI agents in the ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials, of whom the training cohort consisted of 1030 patients, while the internal validation cohort consisted of 688 patients. Overall, 54% (n = 551) in the training cohort, 56% (n = 383) in the internal validation cohort, and 69% (n = 371) in the external validation cohort experienced an early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months.

After the NADIR model (https://bit.ly/42Ec1lP) was built utilizing the training cohort, it was locked and applied to the two validation cohorts. The model coefficients with 95% confidence intervals (CI) are summarized in Table 1. In the internal validation cohort, the AUC for the NADIR model was 0.76 (95% CI = 0.72–0.79) with a Brier score of 0.20. In the external validation cohort, the AUC was 0.82 (95% CI = 0.78–0.85) with a Brier score of 0.16. The receiver operating curves are shown in Fig. 2. The calibration plots showed alignment between the predicted probabilities and the actual outcomes in the training, internal and external validation cohorts (Supplementary Figs. S1, S2, S3, respectively, in the supplementary information). In the external validation cohort, the sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV of the model were 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.86), 0.62 (95% CI = 0.54–0.69), 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.86), and 0.62 (95% CI = 0.54–0.69), respectively (Supplementary Table S2, supplementary information). On LOOCV, the model demonstrated consistent performance (AUC values ranging between 0.78 and 0.82; Brier scores ranging from 0.16 to 0.19) across trials (Supplementary Table S3, supplementary information). There was substantial heterogeneity in the distribution of predicted probability of achieving early PSA response based on metastatic volume by CHAARTED definition across the internal validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S4, supplementary information) and external validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S5, supplementary information), respectively. Removing baseline PSA from the multivariable model led to a substantial drop in predictive accuracy in external validation, confirming PSA as an important predictor but not a sufficient one (Table 2). Importantly, the full NADIR model outperformed PSA-only model across exploratory subgroups within the external validation cohort stratified by baseline PSA levels with greater benefits among patients with baseline PSA value higher than 5 ng/mL (Supplementary Table S4, supplementary information).

Quartile-based stratification demonstrated similar differences in the proportion of patients with early favorable PSA responses in the internal and external validation cohort, respectively (Supplementary Figs. S8 and S9, supplementary information). On decision curve analysis in the external validation cohort, the NADIR model was most useful for identifying patients at a range of risk that is clinically meaningful (threshold probabilities between 25% and 60%) for early PSA drop in patients treated with ARPI with a higher net benefit in this range compared to both baseline assumptions (no patient has early PSA response, and all patients have early PSA response) (Supplementary Fig. S10, supplementary information).

The 4-years OS probabilities in patients stratified by tertiles of predicted probability were 71% (95% CI = 65–79); 61% (95% CI = 55–69); and 47% (95% CI = 39–56), respectively in the internal validation cohort (n = 672) (Fig. 3) and 80% (95% CI = 75–86), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 56% (95% CI = 49–64), respectively in the external validation cohort (n = 540) (Fig. 4). As an exploratory analysis, we applied the NADIR model on patients treated with ADT with/without docetaxel. ## Methods

Studycohorts
Our research complies with all relevant ethical regulations by the institutional review board of University Hospitals Seidman Cancer Center (STUDY20251115) and data-sharing agreements with trial sponsors. All patients provided informed consent before they were enrolled in the respective trials. A literature search was performed using Medline and Clinicaltrials.gov to identify phase III randomized controlled trials of patients solely with mHSPC randomized to ADT with or without an ARPI, irrespective of docetaxel use. Each trial group or industry partner was contacted to obtain IPD. Four trials met criteria for which IPD access was granted for analysis: ARASENS (NCT02799602), ENZAMET (NCT02446405), LATITUDE (NCT01715285), and TITAN (NCT02489318). For ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN, data were accessed via a peer-reviewed data access request on the Vivli platform (Project ID: 009912), while data from the ENZAMET (NCT02446405) trial were accessed through the Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group. This post-hoc analysis was conducted in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan approved by all relevant parties.

Patients eligible for this analysis were adult (≥18 years) patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed mHSPC, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status score of 0 or 1, and evidence of metastases on bone scans or cross-sectional imaging. All study participants were male, and sex was determined by clinical diagnosis. Patients were included if they were randomly assigned to and treated with ADT with or without docetaxel plus ARPI and had complete baseline and follow-up data for clinical outcomes, treatment assignments, and baseline (pre-ARPI) demographic and clinical characteristics, and laboratory variables such as age (in years), body mass index (BMI), metastatic disease volume (high versus low per CHAARTED criteria)9,10, visceral metastases (yes/no), baseline PSA (ng/mL), hemoglobin (g/L), docetaxel use (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous), respectively. All analyzes complied with the terms set by the data providers, and no identifiable patient information was used.

Statisticsandreproducibility
The primary endpoint was early favorable PSA response, defined as a decline in serum PSA level to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of random allocation among patients treated with an ARPI. Patients from ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials were pooled and randomly split into training (60%) and internal validation (40%) cohorts using unstratified random allocation. We used a 60:40 split to prioritize a larger training cohort for model development, ensuring stable coefficient estimation while retaining a sufficiently large internal validation cohort for performance testing. The training cohort was used to build the model and once locked, the model’s performance was evaluated in the internal and external validation cohorts.

Model development utilized logistic regression, including baseline PSA fitted with restricted cubic splines with 4 degrees of freedom, log of baseline hemoglobin, baseline body mass index, and age at enrollment respectively, in addition to metastatic disease volume (low versus high by CHAARTED definition)9, visceral metastasis (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous). Variables election was based on clinical relevance, with final model specification determined by the Akaike Information Criterion. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals from 5000 bootstrap iterations. Calibration was evaluated by comparing bootstrapped estimates of early PSA nadir probabilities with 95% confidence intervals across tertiles of predicted probabilities in both internal and external validation cohorts. We selected tertiles to ensure adequate sample sizes and event counts within each subgroup. This avoided over-stratification, which could lead to unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals. Additional performance metrics included Brier score (which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities with lower Brier score indicating better calibration), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and positive and negative likelihood ratio. No pre-specified probability threshold was selected to define clinical actionability; thresholds were explored post hoc to evaluate model performance across a range of values using decision curve analysis. Variable importance was estimated using loss of index of prediction accuracy (IPA). IPA is calculated by rescaling the Brier score.

External validation employed individual patient data from the ARPI arm of the ENZAMET trial to assess the model’s generalizability. A post-hoc power analysis confirmed adequate sample size to detect an AUC of 0.75 with a significance level of 0.05. To determine the validation of our model, we performed a leave-one-trial-out-validation (LOOCV). Each trial was sequentially excluded and used as an external validation cohort while the model was trained on the remaining three trials. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the AUC with 95% confidence intervals. Calibration was evaluated using Brier scores. This approach allows for evaluation of model generalizability and reduces potential overfitting to any single dataset. As an additional sensitivity analysis, a random forest classifier was developed and evaluated using the same framework.

Given the prognostic implications of early PSA response, overall survival (OS) was explored in a 6-month landmark population stratified by tertiles (upper, middle, and lower) of predicted probability from the NADIR model. Overall survival (OS) was reported at 4 years because follow-up beyond 4 years was limited in the training and validation cohorts. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated hazard of deaths across the tertiles, and the potential differential effect of docetaxel based on predicted probabilities from the NADIR model using an interaction term. Proportionality assumption was tested using Grambsch–Therneau test. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was made, and all reported p-values were 2-sided. All statistical analyzes were performed using R version 4.4.1 with its associated packages (tidymodels, tidyverse, pROC, riskRegression, survival, rms)37–40.

## Methods

Studycohorts
Our research complies with all relevant ethical regulations by the institutional review board of University Hospitals Seidman Cancer Center (STUDY20251115) and data-sharing agreements with trial sponsors. All patients provided informed consent before they were enrolled in the respective trials. A literature search was performed using Medline and Clinicaltrials.gov to identify phase III randomized controlled trials of patients solely with mHSPC randomized to ADT with or without an ARPI, irrespective of docetaxel use. Each trial group or industry partner was contacted to obtain IPD. Four trials met criteria for which IPD access was granted for analysis: ARASENS (NCT02799602), ENZAMET (NCT02446405), LATITUDE (NCT01715285), and TITAN (NCT02489318). For ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN, data were accessed via a peer-reviewed data access request on the Vivli platform (Project ID: 009912), while data from the ENZAMET (NCT02446405) trial were accessed through the Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group. This post-hoc analysis was conducted in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan approved by all relevant parties.

Patients eligible for this analysis were adult (≥18 years) patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed mHSPC, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status score of 0 or 1, and evidence of metastases on bone scans or cross-sectional imaging. All study participants were male, and sex was determined by clinical diagnosis. Patients were included if they were randomly assigned to and treated with ADT with or without docetaxel plus ARPI and had complete baseline and follow-up data for clinical outcomes, treatment assignments, and baseline (pre-ARPI) demographic and clinical characteristics, and laboratory variables such as age (in years), body mass index (BMI), metastatic disease volume (high versus low per CHAARTED criteria)9,10, visceral metastases (yes/no), baseline PSA (ng/mL), hemoglobin (g/L), docetaxel use (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous), respectively. All analyzes complied with the terms set by the data providers, and no identifiable patient information was used.

Statisticsandreproducibility
The primary endpoint was early favorable PSA response, defined as a decline in serum PSA level to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of random allocation among patients treated with an ARPI. Patients from ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials were pooled and randomly split into training (60%) and internal validation (40%) cohorts using unstratified random allocation. We used a 60:40 split to prioritize a larger training cohort for model development, ensuring stable coefficient estimation while retaining a sufficiently large internal validation cohort for performance testing. The training cohort was used to build the model and once locked, the model’s performance was evaluated in the internal and external validation cohorts.

Model development utilized logistic regression, including baseline PSA fitted with restricted cubic splines with 4 degrees of freedom, log of baseline hemoglobin, baseline body mass index, and age at enrollment respectively, in addition to metastatic disease volume (low versus high by CHAARTED definition)9, visceral metastasis (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous). Variables election was based on clinical relevance, with final model specification determined by the Akaike Information Criterion. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals from 5000 bootstrap iterations. Calibration was evaluated by comparing bootstrapped estimates of early PSA nadir probabilities with 95% confidence intervals across tertiles of predicted probabilities in both internal and external validation cohorts. We selected tertiles to ensure adequate sample sizes and event counts within each subgroup. This avoided over-stratification, which could lead to unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals. Additional performance metrics included Brier score (which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities with lower Brier score indicating better calibration), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and positive and negative likelihood ratio. No pre-specified probability threshold was selected to define clinical actionability; thresholds were explored post hoc to evaluate model performance across a range of values using decision curve analysis. Variable importance was estimated using loss of index of prediction accuracy (IPA). IPA is calculated by rescaling the Brier score.

External validation employed individual patient data from the ARPI arm of the ENZAMET trial to assess the model’s generalizability. A post-hoc power analysis confirmed adequate sample size to detect an AUC of 0.75 with a significance level of 0.05. To determine the validation of our model, we performed a leave-one-trial-out-validation (LOOCV). Each trial was sequentially excluded and used as an external validation cohort while the model was trained on the remaining three trials. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the AUC with 95% confidence intervals. Calibration was evaluated using Brier scores. This approach allows for evaluation of model generalizability and reduces potential overfitting to any single dataset. As an additional sensitivity analysis, a random forest classifier was developed and evaluated using the same framework.

Given the prognostic implications of early PSA response, overall survival (OS) was explored in a 6-month landmark population stratified by tertiles (upper, middle, and lower) of predicted probability from the NADIR model. Overall survival (OS) was reported at 4 years because follow-up beyond 4 years was limited in the training and validation cohorts. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated hazard of deaths across the tertiles, and the potential differential effect of docetaxel based on predicted probabilities from the NADIR model using an interaction term. Proportionality assumption was tested using Grambsch–Therneau test. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was made, and all reported p-values were 2-sided. All statistical analyzes were performed using R version 4.4.1 with its associated packages (tidymodels, tidyverse, pROC, riskRegression, survival, rms)37–40.

## Paper

## Abstract

There is an unmet need for a tool that could predict early favorable prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) patients receiving androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI). Here, we train and validate a multivariable logistic regression model to predict early favorable PSA response (≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months) in these patients. Patients randomly allocated to the ARPI arms of the LATITUDE (abiraterone), TITAN (apalutamide), and ARASENS (darolutamide) trials, are split 60:40 into training (n = 1030) and internal validation (n = 688) cohorts. The locked model is validated in an independent external validation cohort - the enzalutamide arm of the ENZAMET trial (n = 540). The area under curve and Brier score for the locked model in the external validation cohort are 0.82 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.78–0.85) and 0.16, respectively. Stratification by predicted probability tertiles show PSA response rates of 92% (95% CI = 88–96), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 39% (95% CI = 32–47), respectively. Pending prospective validation, our model predicts early favorable PSA response supporting its potential role in guiding treatment decisions.

---

## Introduction

Early PSA response is a well-established prognostic marker in metastatic hormone sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) patients treated with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) alone or a combination of ADT plus androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPI) with or without docetaxel1–7. Achieving a PSA response of ≤0.2 ng/mL within 6 months of treatment initiation predicts improved overall survival (OS) and mediates the treatment effect on subsequent mortality risk8. Conversely, failure to reach this response threshold portends inferior OS. Therefore, this clinical state may warrant an earlier treatment intensification, or a clinical trial enrollment. However, waiting until 6 months to assess PSA nadir may inadvertently delay timely intervention, allowing disease progression and evolution to a more treatment-resistant state, potentially diminishing the benefit of subsequent therapeutic intensification. Predicting PSA responses using pre-treatment variables, especially in ARPI-treated patients, could enable earlier, personalized treatment decisions before the optimal intervention window closes.

Conventional risk stratification methods in mHSPC, such as volume of metastatic disease based on conventional imaging9,10, have limited accuracy in predicting early PSA response. For example, one study demonstrated that over half of patients with favorable PSA responses had high-volume metastatic disease, while nearly 1/3 of those with suboptimal PSA response had low-volume disease8. These findings underscore the limitations of relying on a single variable for risk stratification and treatment optimization in mHSPC.

Therefore, there is an unmet need of an easily deployable clinical tool, which could predict favorable early PSA response. While such tool will not be a replacement for formal PSA monitoring, it will provide baseline prognostic insights that can enhance early risk stratification, guide treatment planning, and support enrollment in biomarker-driven studies.

In this work, we developed and validated the Nadir ARPI-Derived Integrative Response (NADIR) model using individual patient data from four phase III trials (ARASENS, ENZAMET, LATITUDE, and TITAN)11–14. This tool leverages pretreatment clinical and laboratory parameters to estimate the likelihood of achieving a PSA ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of initiating ARPI-based therapy.

---

## Results

Baseline characteristics
Overall, 1718 male patients were treated with ARPI agents in the ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials, of whom the training cohort consisted of 1030 patients, while the internal validation cohort consisted of 688 patients. The external validation cohort consisted of 540 male patients from the ENZAMET trial (Fig. 1). Baseline characteristics have been summarized in Supplementary Table S1 (supplementary information). Overall, 54% (n = 551) in the training cohort, 56% (n = 383) in the internal validation cohort, and 69% (n = 371) in the external validation cohort experienced an early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months.

Modeltrainingandvalidation
After the NADIR model (https://bit.ly/42Ec1lP) was built utilizing the training cohort, it was locked and applied to the two validation cohorts. The model coefficients with 95% confidence intervals (CI) are summarized in Table 1. In the internal validation cohort, the AUC for the NADIR model was 0.76 (95% CI = 0.72–0.79) with a Brier score of 0.20. In the external validation cohort, the AUC was 0.82 (95% CI = 0.78–0.85) with a Brier score of 0.16. The receiver operating curves are shown in Fig. 2. The calibration plots showed alignment between the predicted probabilities and the actual outcomes in the training, internal and external validation cohorts (Supplementary Figs. S1, S2, S3, respectively, in the supplementary information). In the external validation cohort, the sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV of the model were 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.86), 0.62 (95% CI = 0.54–0.69), 0.83 (95% CI = 0.79–0.86), and 0.62 (95% CI = 0.54–0.69), respectively (Supplementary Table S2, supplementary information). On LOOCV, the model demonstrated consistent performance (AUC values ranging between 0.78 and 0.82; Brier scores ranging from 0.16 to 0.19) across trials (Supplementary Table S3, supplementary information). There was substantial heterogeneity in the distribution of predicted probability of achieving early PSA response based on metastatic volume by CHAARTED definition across the internal validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S4, supplementary information) and external validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S5, supplementary information), respectively. Removing baseline PSA from the multivariable model led to a substantial drop in predictive accuracy in external validation, confirming PSA as an important predictor but not a sufficient one (Table 2). Importantly, the full NADIR model outperformed PSA-only model across exploratory subgroups within the external validation cohort stratified by baseline PSA levels with greater benefits among patients with baseline PSA value higher than 5 ng/mL (Supplementary Table S4, supplementary information).

RiskstratificationbyNADIRmodel
When stratified by decreasing order of tertiles of predicted probability of early PSA response, the proportions achieving a favorable early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL in the upper (n = 229), middle (n = 229), and lower tertile (n = 230) were 83% (95% CI = 78–88), 52% (95% CI = 46–59), and 32% (95% CI = 26–38) in the internal validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S6, supplementary information). Similarly, the proportions achieving a favorable early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL in the upper (n = 180), middle (n = 180), and lower tertile (n = 180) were 92% (95% CI = 88–96), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 39% (95% CI = 32–47) in the external validation cohort (Supplementary Fig. S7, supplementary information). Quartile-based stratification demonstrated similar differences in the proportion of patients with early favorable PSA responses in the internal and external validation cohort, respectively (Supplementary Figs. S8 and S9, supplementary information). On decision curve analysis in the external validation cohort, the NADIR model was most useful for identifying patients at a range of risk that is clinically meaningful (threshold probabilities between 25% and 60%) for early PSA drop in patients treated with ARPI with a higher net benefit in this range compared to both baseline assumptions (no patient has early PSA response, and all patients have early PSA response) (Supplementary Fig. S10, supplementary information).

We subsequently determined the OS estimates across the tertiles of predicted probability from the NADIR model using Kaplan–Meier methods. The 4-years OS probabilities in patients stratified by tertiles of predicted probability were 71% (95% CI = 65–79); 61% (95% CI = 55–69); and 47% (95% CI = 39–56), respectively in the internal validation cohort (n = 672) (Fig. 3) and 80% (95% CI = 75–86), 74% (95% CI = 68–81), and 56% (95% CI = 49–64), respectively in the external validation cohort (n = 540) (Fig. 4). On Cox proportional hazard regression modeling, compared to upper tertile, patients in the middle and lower tertile had inferior OS in the internal validation cohort (HR for middle tertile = 1.57 [95% CI = 1.11–2.21]; HR for lower tertile = 2.28 [95% CI = 1.65–3.16]) and in the external validation cohort (HR for middle tertile = 1.35 [95% CI = 0.92–1.69]; HR for lower tertile = 2.72 [95% CI = 1.91–3.88], respectively.

Exploratoryanalysisofinteractionwithdocetaxeleffect
In the combined validation cohort, we did not find any considerable evidence of difference in proportion of patients with early PSA response with and without use of docetaxel across the three risk score groups (Supplementary Table S5, supplementary information). We found a differential effect from docetaxel on OS across the predicted scores from the NADIR model (HR for the interaction term 0.41; 95% CI = 0.19–0.88; two-sided p-interaction = 0.0215) (Supplementary Fig. S11, supplementary information). Kaplan–Meier method-based OS estimates with and without docetaxel use in these groups are shown in Supplementary Figs. S12 and S13, respectively (supplementary information). For patients in the lower tertile of predicted probability of early favorable PSA response (n = 401), 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 55% (95% CI = 48–63) and 53% (95% CI = 46–61), respectively while for patients in the upper to middle tertiles (n = 811), the 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 66% (95% CI = 60–72) and 72% (95% CI = 68–77), respectively (Supplementary Fig. S12, supplementary information). For patients in the upper-tertile of predicted probability of early favorable PSA response (n = 408), 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 72% (95% CI = 65–80) and 78% (95% CI = 72–83), respectively while for patients in the lower to middle tertiles (n = 804), 4-year OS estimates with and without docetaxel were 58% (95% CI = 52–63) and 60% (95% CI = 56–65), respectively (Supplementary Fig. S13, supplementary information). Similar evidence of differential treatment effect from on OS across the predicted scores from the NADIR model (HR for the interaction term 0.28; 95% CI = 0.09–0.92; two-sided p-interaction = 0.03377) was found in the external validation cohort (n = 540) (Supplementary Fig. S14, supplementary information).

Additionalsensitivityanalyses
As an exploratory analysis, we applied the NADIR model on patients treated with ADT with/without docetaxel. In patients treated with ADT with/without docetaxel, the AUC of the NADIR model was 0.77 (95% CI = 0.75–0.79) with a Brier score of 0.24. On decision curve analysis, the NADIR model was useful for identifying patients at a range of risk that is clinically meaningful (threshold probabilities between 15% and 50%) for early PSA response to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months (Supplementary Fig. S15, supplementary information). On sensitivity analysis, the random forest classifier model had an AUC and Brier scores similar to the logistic regression model in the internal validation cohort (AUC: 0.75 [95% CI = 0.72–0.80]; Brier score: 0.20) and in the external validation cohort (AUC: 0.83 [95% CI = 0.79–0.86]; Brier score: 0.17), respectively. Additional metrics for the random forest classifier model are summarized in Supplementary Table S6 (supplementary information). The decision curve analysis showed similar net benefit as the logistic regression model when compared to both baseline assumptions (Supplementary Fig. S16, supplementary information).

---

## Methods

Studycohorts
Our research complies with all relevant ethical regulations by the institutional review board of University Hospitals Seidman Cancer Center (STUDY20251115) and data-sharing agreements with trial sponsors. All patients provided informed consent before they were enrolled in the respective trials. A literature search was performed using Medline and Clinicaltrials.gov to identify phase III randomized controlled trials of patients solely with mHSPC randomized to ADT with or without an ARPI, irrespective of docetaxel use. Each trial group or industry partner was contacted to obtain IPD. Four trials met criteria for which IPD access was granted for analysis: ARASENS (NCT02799602), ENZAMET (NCT02446405), LATITUDE (NCT01715285), and TITAN (NCT02489318). For ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN, data were accessed via a peer-reviewed data access request on the Vivli platform (Project ID: 009912), while data from the ENZAMET (NCT02446405) trial were accessed through the Australian and New Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials Group. This post-hoc analysis was conducted in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan approved by all relevant parties.

Patients eligible for this analysis were adult (≥18 years) patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed mHSPC, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status score of 0 or 1, and evidence of metastases on bone scans or cross-sectional imaging. All study participants were male, and sex was determined by clinical diagnosis. Patients were included if they were randomly assigned to and treated with ADT with or without docetaxel plus ARPI and had complete baseline and follow-up data for clinical outcomes, treatment assignments, and baseline (pre-ARPI) demographic and clinical characteristics, and laboratory variables such as age (in years), body mass index (BMI), metastatic disease volume (high versus low per CHAARTED criteria)9,10, visceral metastases (yes/no), baseline PSA (ng/mL), hemoglobin (g/L), docetaxel use (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous), respectively. All analyzes complied with the terms set by the data providers, and no identifiable patient information was used.

Statisticsandreproducibility
The primary endpoint was early favorable PSA response, defined as a decline in serum PSA level to ≤0.2 ng/mL by 6 months of random allocation among patients treated with an ARPI. Patients from ARASENS, LATITUDE, and TITAN trials were pooled and randomly split into training (60%) and internal validation (40%) cohorts using unstratified random allocation. We used a 60:40 split to prioritize a larger training cohort for model development, ensuring stable coefficient estimation while retaining a sufficiently large internal validation cohort for performance testing. The training cohort was used to build the model and once locked, the model’s performance was evaluated in the internal and external validation cohorts.

Model development utilized logistic regression, including baseline PSA fitted with restricted cubic splines with 4 degrees of freedom, log of baseline hemoglobin, baseline body mass index, and age at enrollment respectively, in addition to metastatic disease volume (low versus high by CHAARTED definition)9, visceral metastasis (yes versus no), and metastatic stage at presentation (synchronous versus metachronous). Variables election was based on clinical relevance, with final model specification determined by the Akaike Information Criterion. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals from 5000 bootstrap iterations. Calibration was evaluated by comparing bootstrapped estimates of early PSA nadir probabilities with 95% confidence intervals across tertiles of predicted probabilities in both internal and external validation cohorts. We selected tertiles to ensure adequate sample sizes and event counts within each subgroup. This avoided over-stratification, which could lead to unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals. Additional performance metrics included Brier score (which measures the accuracy of predicted probabilities with lower Brier score indicating better calibration), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and positive and negative likelihood ratio. No pre-specified probability threshold was selected to define clinical actionability; thresholds were explored post hoc to evaluate model performance across a range of values using decision curve analysis. Variable importance was estimated using loss of index of prediction accuracy (IPA). IPA is calculated by rescaling the Brier score.

External validation employed individual patient data from the ARPI arm of the ENZAMET trial to assess the model’s generalizability. A post-hoc power analysis confirmed adequate sample size to detect an AUC of 0.75 with a significance level of 0.05. To determine the validation of our model, we performed a leave-one-trial-out-validation (LOOCV). Each trial was sequentially excluded and used as an external validation cohort while the model was trained on the remaining three trials. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the AUC with 95% confidence intervals. Calibration was evaluated using Brier scores. This approach allows for evaluation of model generalizability and reduces potential overfitting to any single dataset. As an additional sensitivity analysis, a random forest classifier was developed and evaluated using the same framework.

Given the prognostic implications of early PSA response, overall survival (OS) was explored in a 6-month landmark population stratified by tertiles (upper, middle, and lower) of predicted probability from the NADIR model. Overall survival (OS) was reported at 4 years because follow-up beyond 4 years was limited in the training and validation cohorts. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated hazard of deaths across the tertiles, and the potential differential effect of docetaxel based on predicted probabilities from the NADIR model using an interaction term. Proportionality assumption was tested using Grambsch–Therneau test. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was made, and all reported p-values were 2-sided. All statistical analyzes were performed using R version 4.4.1 with its associated packages (tidymodels, tidyverse, pROC, riskRegression, survival, rms)37–40.

Comment 9: Major Comments on Overall Methodology
My biggest question or concern is the lack of justification around why ENZAMET was
specifically used for the external validation dataset. Some commonly established
challenges and drawbacks of using only one trial/database for external validation
(ENZAMET) include the potential for: overfitting risk and reduced generalizability,
especially if additional differences between the internal training/external validation
samples (e.g., patient characteristics, years of trial, etc.)
I would suggest the use of leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), which would
aggregate model fit by using and rotating each of the 4 pivotal trial databases as the
external validation arm, which can help reduce the potential for dataset-specific
overfitting and bolster model generalizability with more equitable model evaluation
across the 4 trial datasets.
